newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition leads protests across Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Opposition leads protests across Serbia.

text.p: Serbian opposition parties led fresh protests on Friday to demand that President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialists accept defeat in local elections.
Despite a light rain, thousands marched through the capital Belgrade before gathering in the city centre to hear speeches from leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition.
"We're not giving up our victory!" chanted the crowd in front of the offices of the opposition Democratic Party.
The poor weather apparently kept some supporters away from the demonstration which drew some 10,000, about half the size of Thursday's protest.
Earlier, some 1,000 Belgrade university students held their own demonstration backing the opposition, which accuses the Socialists of trying to annul their victory in local polls.
The opposition said it organised large demonstrations in four other towns on Friday evening, seeking to keep up pressure on Milosevic to recognise the results.
Opposition leader Zoran Djindjic said Milosevic's rule was under unprecedented threat after the local election and five days of protests across the republic.
"It (the election victory) puts in question the basic principles of his authority," Djindjic told Reuters.
"Milosevic is not losing much in terms of real power but psychologically he's losing a lot. There is going to be a chain reaction," he said.
Djindjic heads the Democratic Party (DS), one of three parties in the Zajedno coalition, and is expected to become the next mayor of Belgrade.
While vowing to continue the protests over the weekend, Djindjic said international support could make the difference between success and failure for the opposition.
"What would help would be to employ the already proven method in which (U.S. President Bill) Clinton or (French President Jacques) Chirac would telephone Milosevic," he said.
International pressure helped force the former communist leader to ditch nationalist war aims and agree a peace settlement in former Yugoslavia one year ago.
Western powers were slow to react to the opposition charges but after several days of protests the United States and Britain have voiced grave concerns about possible fraud.
Opposition leaders say the authorities have committed massive fraud by cancelling votes which gave the opposition victories in 15 of the 18 biggest towns in Serbia at local elections last Sunday.
Analysts say the opposition victory took the Socialists by surprise and prompted them to resort to reversing the results.
Milosevic, whose leftist coalition won in federal elections earlier this month, has kept silent over the protests while his state media has delivered mixed signals.
State television, which initially ignored the demonstrations, has portrayed the opposition as provocateurs who refuse to wait for the outcome of electoral "procedures".

But the television has also broadcast a statement from Nova Democratija (New Democracy), a member of Milosevic's leftist coalition, which denounced election rigging and called for the will of the people to be respected. Its headquarters were bombed hours later.
Courts have yet to deliver rulings on ballot results and opposition leaders said they expected a final decision by Sunday night.
Zajedno officials expressed concern the Socialists were trying to overturn the opposition's victory in Belgrade, which authorities had confirmed on Tuesday.
"Unofficially we have heard that the Socialists have managed to contest another 13 seats in the Belgrade assembly," Dragor Hribar, another Democratic Party leader, told B92 radio.
The Socialists, while challenging poll results elsewhere in Serbia, had previously conceded defeat in Belgrade saying Zajedno had won 60 out of the 110 seats in the city assembly.
